title: Feedlot Health Management Services (Feb 2015 TCC) Case
subject: Third-Party Payments for Supplying Test Cattle Under the Proxy Method
summary: Feedlot Health Management Services Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 32, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for corporations claiming third-party payments under the proxy method. Justice Woods held that $1,649,537 paid to Jim Farms for supplying test cattle qualified under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) as expenditures "in respect of" SR&ED undertaken on the taxpayer's behalf.
metaDescription: Read the February 2015 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Feedlot Health Management Services Ltd. on Canadian SR&ED tax credits.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
1.1 Corporate Context, Experimental Projects, and Contractual Architecture

In Feedlot Health Management Services Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 32 (Docket 2012-1292(IT)G), issued on February 6, 2015, Justice Judith Woods of the Tax Court of Canada adjudicated a pivotal dispute concerning the deductibility and Investment Tax Credit (ITC) eligibility of third-party payments under the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) regime of the Canadian Income Tax Act (the "ITA"). The appellant, Feedlot Health Management Services Ltd. ("FHMS"), is a private corporation headquartered in Okotoks, Alberta, that provides specialized consulting services in veterinary science and beef cattle production. During its 2010 taxation year, FHMS was indirectly owned by four veterinarians, with its largest indirect shareholder—holding a 42.5% equity interest through a holding corporation—being Dr. Gung Kee Jim. Concurrently, Dr. Jim was the sole proprietor of GK Jim Farms ("Jim Farms"), a substantial commercial cattle investment and production enterprise.

During the 2010 taxation year, FHMS executed four research projects on behalf of sponsors to test the relationship between new diets, supplements, and vaccines and the health and performance of beef cattle. Across the four projects, approximately 7,000 head of cattle owned by third parties were subjected to controlled experimental protocols over several months inside commercial feedlots before being shipped to commercial meat-packing plants (abattoirs) for slaughter and sale. While the cattle were raised for commercial beef production using standard husbandry practices, those practices were systematically modified to conform to the experimental designs mandated by FHMS.

To execute these field trials, FHMS entered into contractual arrangements with two distinct categories of counterparties. First, FHMS entered into Cooperator Agreements directly with the commercial feedlot operators housing the cattle. Under these Cooperator Agreements, the feedlots conducted work in relation to the projects, including administering the particular diets, supplements, and vaccines required by the projects, taking measurements of the cattle throughout the process, and transmitting the resulting data to FHMS for analysis.

Second, to secure the test animals, FHMS entered into four separate Research Study Agreements (RSAs)—one per project—with Dr. Jim's sole proprietorship, Jim Farms, which supplied a large percentage of the 7,000 test cattle. Under a representative contract (Study FHMS 0803), Jim Farms agreed to acquire at its own expense approximately 3,930 head of exotic crossbred steers from auction markets matching specific baseline health and breed criteria suitable for evaluating wheat- and corn-based dry distiller's grains plus solubles (DDGS) in finishing rations. Jim Farms agreed to request that the cattle be processed to FHMS's specifications and to pay all initial acquisition costs, transportation expenses to the participating feedlots, and feeding costs during the initial evaluation period in which FHMS evaluated whether the animals met study requirements. Upon acceptance of cattle into a study, FHMS agreed to pay all feeding and health costs associated with the study cattle; the RSAs also granted FHMS access to all health and carcass data and provided that all health, feeding, and marketing decisions for the study animals would be made by FHMS—which, as the Court understood it, generally meant that the cattle would be processed at specific times to accommodate the projects. In exchange, FHMS paid Jim Farms an aggregate sum of $1,649,537 across the four RSAs during the 2010 taxation year.
1.2 The Tax Authority's Challenge and the Governing Statutory Framework

In filing its 2010 T2 corporate income tax return and Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), FHMS elected to compute its SR&ED expenditures under the simplified proxy method pursuant to clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA, claiming the $1,649,537 paid to Jim Farms as qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for current deduction under subsection 37(1) and ITCs under section 127.

Unlike the traditional method of SR&ED accounting under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)—which permits taxpayers to deduct all expenditures of a current nature that are "all or substantially all" attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED alongside overhead expenses—the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) is intended to exclude certain expenditures such as overhead and, in their place, to allow a percentage of SR&ED-related salaries and wages for ITC purposes, and it restricts qualifying expenditures to an exhaustive statutory list of six enumerated clauses, designated as clauses (I) through (VI). For the 2010 taxation year at issue, clause (I) encompassed current expenditures all or substantially all of which were attributable to the lease of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, and clause (VI) encompassed one-half of any other current expenditure in respect of the lease of premises, facilities, or equipment used primarily for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Clause (II) covered expenditures in respect of the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer. Clause (III) addressed capital expenditures for the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment described in subclause (A)(III), while Clause (IV) governed the portion of salary or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada that can reasonably be considered to relate to such work, and Clause (V) captured the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Underlying all expenditure computations under section 37 is the gateway statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which encompasses basic research, applied research, and experimental development under paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(c) and includes specific supporting work such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research under paragraph 248(1)(d) where such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of work described in paragraphs (a)–(c). Simultaneously, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes enumerated activities under paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k), including market research, routine testing, social science research, mineral and petroleum exploration, style changes, and routine data collection. Most notably for agricultural and industrial trials, paragraph 248(1)(i) excludes any work with respect to "the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process".

Upon audit, the Minister of National Revenue, acting through the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA"), conceded the scientific validity of the underlying projects. Specifically, the Minister accepted that all four veterinary research projects satisfied the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1), and further accepted that the activities performed by the commercial feedlots under the Cooperator Agreements—administering experimental treatments and collecting biometric data—constituted eligible third-party SR&ED work. However, the Minister disallowed the entirety of the $1,649,537 paid to Jim Farms under the RSAs. The Crown maintained that Jim Farms performed no SR&ED work under paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(d), that the raising and fattening of Jim Farms' cattle constituted excluded commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i), and that the payments to Jim Farms failed to qualify under any enumerated category of the proxy method in clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B).
1.3 The Tax Court of Canada's Final Holding

Justice Woods delivered a nuanced, multi-part judgment that rejected the taxpayer's equipment lease theory and commented that Jim Farms' own work was caught by the commercial exclusion, yet ultimately allowed the appeal in full with costs under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II)—a provision FHMS had pleaded in its Notice of Appeal but chose not to pursue during argument, and which the Court revived of its own motion after the hearing. First, the Court rejected the taxpayer's equipment lease theory, holding that the RSAs did not constitute a "lease of equipment" under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) or (VI). Without deciding whether cattle could constitute "equipment," the Court held that the RSAs were not leases because a lease implies exclusive possession. Because FHMS did not have exclusive possession of the cattle and had only limited rights with respect to them, while Jim Farms retained some rights throughout the period of the RSAs, no lease existed.

Second, in comments that the Court described as unnecessary to the result, Justice Woods indicated that the work undertaken by Jim Farms under the RSAs—although otherwise SR&ED as work with respect to testing and data collection under paragraph 248(1)(d)—was excluded from the definition of SR&ED by virtue of paragraph 248(1)(i), because activities such as acquiring the cattle and permitting FHMS to determine feed and supplement protocols were also exploited by Jim Farms in its ordinary business of raising cattle.

Third, the Court found that the disputed expenditures nevertheless qualified under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) as expenditures "in respect of" third-party SR&ED. Invoking the Supreme Court of Canada's framework in R. v. Mian, 2014 SCC 54, Justice Woods requested post-hearing supplementary submissions on clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II), which covers expenditures "in respect of the prosecution of scientific research and experimental development in Canada directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer". Applying the expansive Supreme Court jurisprudence in The Queen v. Savage, [1983] 2 SCR 428, and Nowegijick v. The Queen, [1983] 1 SCR 29, Justice Woods held that the words "in respect of" carry the widest possible scope. While Clause (II) is restricted to contexts where SR&ED is undertaken by a third party on behalf of the taxpayer, the commercial feedlots were performing recognized third-party SR&ED—testing and data collection under paragraph 248(1)(d)—on behalf of FHMS. Because the sole purpose of FHMS's payments to Jim Farms was to procure and deliver test subject cattle to those feedlots so that the third-party SR&ED data collection could occur, the $1,649,537 expenditure was incurred "in respect of" the prosecution of SR&ED undertaken on behalf of FHMS.

Finally, Justice Woods imposed a procedural bar against the Crown's late-stage challenge to the quantum of the expenditures. Although the Crown argued that some of the disputed expenditures did not relate to SR&ED because their quantum was excessive in relation to the work undertaken by Jim Farms for the projects, Justice Woods declined to consider this reasonableness challenge because the Crown had not raised it as an issue in its Reply to the Notice of Appeal. The entire $1,649,537 deduction was therefore sustained, and the assessment was referred back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment.
2. Core Legal, Contractual, and Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous forensic examination of Feedlot Health Management Services Ltd. v. The Queen reveals that the taxpayer's position was complicated by pre-litigation contractual and tax-planning missteps, and that the dispute was further shaped during litigation by flawed statutory interpretations and procedural pleading omissions by the Crown.
2.1 Pre-Litigation Contractual Mischaracterization and Abandonment of the Materials Consumed Claim

A significant evidentiary deficiency revealed at trial was a contradiction between the written terms of the Research Study Agreements and the actual commercial and financial conduct of FHMS and Jim Farms. On their face, the written RSAs explicitly stipulated that once Jim Farms' cattle passed initial screening and were accepted into a research study, FHMS would pay all feeding and health costs associated with the study cattle. In the Crown's pleaded assumptions in its Reply, it was assumed that FHMS had paid all of the feed costs for three of the projects and half of the feed costs for the fourth project.

At trial, however, Dr. Jim testified that the written payment mechanics in the RSAs did not reflect what actually transpired in practice. In reality, according to Dr. Jim, FHMS paid all of the feed costs in only one project, and FHMS and Jim Farms had negotiated fees equal to a fixed price per head of cattle sufficient to compensate Jim Farms for the risks it took with respect to the RSAs. In three of the four projects, the amounts actually paid by FHMS were significantly less than the entire feeding costs of the cattle, a point the Court accepted.

According to Dr. Jim's testimony, the negotiated per-head price was not reflected in the RSAs because tax advice had been given that the consideration should be linked to feed consumed. The suggestion was that the $1,649,537 be claimed as "materials consumed" in the prosecution of SR&ED under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), and this is how FHMS's tax returns were prepared.

This pre-litigation tax strategy proved problematic on both substantive and evidentiary grounds. Substantively, the Court did not adjudicate the "materials consumed" characterization because FHMS did not attempt to justify it; however, under the CRA's administrative policy, materials are generally regarded as "consumed" only where they are destroyed or rendered virtually worthless by the SR&ED, which sits uneasily with cattle feed eaten by commercial steers owned by a third party that are later sold by that third party to a packing plant. Evidentiarily, Justice Woods found it troublesome that the written agreements between closely connected parties—FHMS and the sole proprietorship of the owner of its 42.5% shareholder—did not reflect the true negotiated arrangement, observing that on its face the testimony suggested that Dr. Jim and FHMS may have intentionally not reflected the true arrangement in the RSAs. Moreover, while Dr. Jim suggested in his testimony that the contractual discrepancy was an inadvertent error, Justice Woods explicitly noted that this testimony was self-interested and viewed his testimony with particular caution, although she accepted the many uncontroversial and unchallenged parts of it, including the testimony about the negotiated fees.
2.2 Failure of the Equipment Lease Argument and the Requirement of Exclusive Possession

Having abandoned the "materials consumed" characterization on which its tax return was prepared, FHMS submitted at trial that the disputed RSA payments qualified under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI) as current expenditures attributable to the lease of equipment—specifically arguing that live experimental cattle constituted "equipment" leased by FHMS from Jim Farms.

Justice Woods rejected this argument by applying the ordinary meaning of "lease," drawing on the Canadian Oxford Dictionary definition and foundational Canadian law governing the legal nature of a lease. Citing the Supreme Court of Canada decision in Johnson v. British Canadian Insurance Company, [1932] SCR 680, Justice Woods emphasized that a lease inherently implies the grant of exclusive possession of the leased property.

An examination of the evidentiary record and the operational reality of the RSAs demonstrated that FHMS did not have exclusive possession of the cattle during the period of the RSAs and had only limited rights with respect to them. The cattle were acquired by Jim Farms and transported to commercial feedlots, which invoiced Jim Farms for feed, yardage, bedding, health, and rendering, and Dr. Jim's testimony suggested that Jim Farms retained some rights with respect to the cattle throughout the period of the RSAs. Throughout the experimental period, the cattle were raised and processed for Jim Farms' cattle investment business in its regular course of operations, subject only to modifications required to accommodate FHMS's research protocols. The rights acquired by FHMS under the RSAs were strictly limited to contractual privileges: the right to dictate health, feeding, and marketing decisions to fit project needs, and the right to access health and carcass data. Justice Woods concluded that it would stretch the meaning of "lease" beyond a reasonable interpretation to encompass the limited non-possessory rights that FHMS acquired under the RSAs, disqualifying the expenditures under clauses (I) and (VI).
2.3 Application of the Commercial Production Exclusion under Paragraph 248(1)(i)

A significant technical issue addressed in the appeal—although the Court considered it only briefly and stated it was not necessary to decide in light of its Clause (II) conclusion—was how the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1)—and specifically the commercial production exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(i)—applies when experimental trials are superimposed upon biological or industrial assets undergoing simultaneous commercial production. Under subsection 248(1), eligible SR&ED comprises basic research, applied research, or experimental development under paragraphs (a)–(c), as well as enumerated supporting work under paragraph (d) such as data collection and testing that is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of work described in paragraphs (a)–(c). However, paragraph 248(1)(i) overrides paragraphs (a)–(d) by explicitly excluding from SR&ED any work with respect to "the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process".

In evaluating whether the work performed directly by Jim Farms qualified as SR&ED, Justice Woods examined the functional nature of Jim Farms' operations. Under the RSAs, Jim Farms acquired cattle at auction, placed them in commercial feedlots, permitted FHMS to establish feed and supplement protocols, and ultimately sold the finished cattle to commercial packing houses in essentially the same commercial manner as any other cattle raised by Jim Farms. While these activities benefited FHMS's research, they were simultaneously exploited by Jim Farms in its regular commercial cattle-raising business. Because a sufficient number of the activities under the RSAs were connected with, and integrated into, Jim Farms' regular commercial business, Justice Woods commented that the work performed by Jim Farms—although otherwise SR&ED as work with respect to testing and data collection under paragraph 248(1)(d)—fell under the commercial exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(i), noting that the exclusion applies to commercial use by a third party as well as by the taxpayer and that each case depends on its own facts.
2.4 Statutory Scope of Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) and the Nexus to Third-Party SR&ED

Because FHMS did not attempt to justify its "materials consumed" filing position, its equipment-leasing argument failed, and it had chosen not to pursue clause (II) during argument despite having pleaded it in its Notice of Appeal, Justice Woods concluded after the hearing, pursuant to the principles in R. v. Mian, 2014 SCC 54, that clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) should be considered and invited supplementary written submissions on its applicability.

Clause (II) permits a taxpayer electing the proxy method to deduct "an expenditure in respect of the prosecution of scientific research and experimental development in Canada directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer". In the supplementary briefing, the Court rejected key aspects of both parties' interpretations of the statutory mechanics of Clause (II). Counsel for FHMS argued overly broadly that Clause (II) applies whenever expenditures relate to SR&ED performed by the taxpayer itself, even if there is no third-party SR&ED contract. Justice Woods rejected this interpretation as incompatible with the text and the statutory structure of the proxy method, concluding that Parliament likely intended Clause (II) to apply only to expenditures in respect of SR&ED where the SR&ED itself is undertaken by a third party on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, the Crown argued that Clause (II) could not apply because the recipient of the payments—Jim Farms—did not perform SR&ED work. Justice Woods rejected the Crown's narrow reading by analyzing the statutory phrase "in respect of". Citing the Supreme Court of Canada's landmark decisions in The Queen v. Savage and Nowegijick v. The Queen, Justice Woods emphasized that "in respect of" is an expression of the widest possible scope, importing meanings such as "in relation to," "with reference to," or "in connection with". Consequently, qualifying expenditures under Clause (II) do not have to be incurred directly for SR&ED per se, nor does the work performed directly by the payee need to be SR&ED, provided the expenditures relate to SR&ED undertaken on the taxpayer's behalf by a third party.

Applying this statutory standard to FHMS's tripartite operational structure established the decisive legal link. Under the Cooperator Agreements, the commercial feedlots performed third-party SR&ED—administering tests and performing data collection under paragraph 248(1)(d)—directly on behalf of FHMS. The sole purpose of the $1,649,537 paid by FHMS to Jim Farms under the RSAs was to facilitate the research projects by arranging for test subject cattle to be delivered to those specific feedlots so that the feedlots could administer the experimental protocols and collect the scientific data. Because the payments provided the biological test subjects required for the feedlots' third-party SR&ED data collection, the payments to Jim Farms were expenditures incurred "in respect of" third-party SR&ED undertaken on behalf of FHMS, satisfying clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II).
2.5 The Crown's Procedural Pleading Deficiencies Regarding Quantum Reasonableness and Commercial Work

A critical takeaway for Canadian tax litigators and SR&ED advisors in 2015 TCC 32 is how the Crown's own pleading failures prevented the Court from reducing or disallowing the claim on quantum grounds. In its supplementary submissions on Clause (II), the Crown argued that a portion of the $1,649,537 paid to Jim Farms did not relate to SR&ED because the quantum was excessive in relation to the work undertaken by Jim Farms for the projects. Justice Woods acknowledged that the evidence appeared to provide some support for the Crown's position; the Court did not specify which evidence, although the record included the related-party relationship (Dr. Jim's sole ownership of Jim Farms and his wholly-owned corporation's 42.5% shareholding in FHMS) and the discrepancies between the written RSAs and the actual per-head fees paid. However, FHMS had explicitly raised the reasonableness of the expenditures in its Notice of Appeal, whereas the Crown chose not to challenge or plead the reasonableness of the expenditures in its Reply. Justice Woods held that FHMS was correct to conclude that reasonableness was not at issue in the appeal, declined to consider the Crown's quantum argument, and assumed for purposes of the decision that the full $1,649,537 was reasonable in relation to the work performed for FHMS.

Additionally, Justice Woods made two preliminary comments about how the Crown pleaded the commercial exclusion under paragraph 248(1)(i) in its Reply. In its Reply, the Crown asserted that "the Payments for feed for – and raising of – the feedlot cattle in the 4 Projects were attributable to the commercial production of improved Farms' feedlot cattle or the commercial use of an improved process for raising Farms' feedlot cattle". First, Justice Woods observed that the Crown improperly focused its pleading on "Payments," whereas the commercial exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(i) relates strictly to the work performed, not the financial consideration paid. Second, by referring to "improved" commercial cattle or an "improved" process, the Crown's pleading incorrectly implied that the research had already been proven, whereas in reality the experimental feeding and health protocols were "new"—although the Court noted that nothing turned on this because paragraph 248(1)(i) also refers to "new" products and processes.
3. Comparative Summary Table of Legal Requirements, Evidentiary Failures, and Judicial Standards

The following table maps each statutory requirement and legal doctrine examined in Feedlot Health Management Services Ltd. v. The Queen against the specific evidentiary, contractual, or procedural failures exhibited by the parties and the authoritative standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada.

Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: Proxy Method: Materials Consumed ITA s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)
Deductibility under the proxy method for the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Taxpayer Failure: On tax advice that the consideration should be linked to feed consumed, the written RSAs stated that FHMS would pay all feeding and health costs of accepted study cattle, whereas in reality FHMS and Jim Farms had negotiated a fixed price per head to compensate Jim Farms for its risks, and in three of the four projects the amounts actually paid were significantly less than the entire feeding costs. The tax returns claimed the amounts as materials consumed, but FHMS did not attempt to justify that filing in the appeal.

The Court did not rule on the materials-consumed characterization. It found troublesome that the RSAs did not reflect the true arrangement and viewed Dr. Jim's self-interested testimony that the discrepancy was "inadvertent" with particular caution, while still accepting his unchallenged testimony that actual payments were significantly less than stated in three projects.
Proxy Method: Lease of Equipment ITA s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) & (VI)

Current expenditures all or substantially all attributable to the lease of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (clause (I)), or one-half of other current lease expenditures for premises, facilities, or equipment used primarily for SR&ED (clause (VI)).

Taxpayer Failure: FHMS argued that third-party cattle were "equipment" and the RSAs were "leases". However, FHMS did not have exclusive possession of the steers, acquiring only limited contractual rights to make health, feeding, and marketing decisions and to access data, while Jim Farms retained some rights with respect to the cattle.

Relying on Johnson v. British Canadian Insurance Company, [1932] SCR 680, a "lease" implies exclusive possession. Contractual access rights and protocol control over a third party's commercial biological assets do not constitute a lease; the Court did not need to decide whether cattle are "equipment".
Commercial Production Exclusion ITA s. 248(1)(i)
Excludes from the definition of SR&ED any work with respect to the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.

Taxpayer Failure: Jim Farms raised and sold the test cattle to commercial packing plants in the regular course of its cattle investment business, which—in the Court's obiter comments—brought Jim Farms' own activities within the exclusion. Crown Failure: The Crown erroneously applied para. 248(1)(i) to payments rather than work, and prematurely labelled unproven experimental protocols as "improved" rather than "new" (although nothing turned on the latter point, since the exclusion covers both).

In obiter, the Court indicated that work of an asset owner that is integrated with, and exploited in, its regular commercial production is excluded from being SR&ED "work" under para. 248(1)(i), including where the commercial use is by a third party; each case depends on its facts. However, para. 248(1)(i) evaluates the work performed, not the payments made, and cannot automatically bar ancillary expenditures that qualify under Clause (II).
Supporting Work: Testing & Data Collection ITA s. 248(1)(d)
Includes work undertaken directly in support of basic/applied research or experimental development (paras. (a)–(c)), specifically including data collection and testing commensurate with those needs.

Taxpayer Success / Crown Concession: FHMS properly structured separate Cooperator Agreements with the commercial feedlots to administer experimental diets/vaccines, measure biometric responses, and transmit experimental data.

The Minister accepted that the work performed by the feedlots under the Cooperator Agreements was SR&ED, and the Court treated the feedlots' data collection as SR&ED undertaken on behalf of FHMS. The Court also commented that Jim Farms' work would otherwise qualify under para. 248(1)(d) as work with respect to testing and data collection, but for the para. 248(1)(i) exclusion.
Proxy Method: Third-Party SR&ED ("In Respect Of") ITA s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II)
Deductibility of an expenditure "in respect of the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer".

Taxpayer Partial Failure: FHMS pleaded Clause (II) in its Notice of Appeal but chose not to pursue it during argument, until the Judge revived it under R. v. Mian, and then argued overly broadly that Clause (II) required no third-party SR&ED. Crown Failure: The Crown argued Clause (II) required Jim Farms itself to perform SR&ED work.

Clause (II) requires that SR&ED be undertaken by a third party on the taxpayer's behalf. However, per Savage and Nowegijick, "in respect of" has the widest possible scope. Payments to a non-SR&ED entity (Jim Farms) solely to supply test subjects to a third-party SR&ED contractor (the feedlots) qualify as expenditures "in respect of" third-party SR&ED.
Reasonableness of Expenditure Quantum ITA s. 67 & Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure)
An expenditure is deductible only to the extent that the quantum is reasonable in the circumstances; issues in dispute must be explicitly pleaded in the Crown's Reply.

Crown Fatal Procedural Failure: Despite the close relationship between the parties (Dr. Jim's wholly-owned corporation held 42.5% of FHMS and Dr. Jim owned 100% of Jim Farms) and discrepant RSA fee calculations, the Crown failed to plead quantum reasonableness in its Reply.

Where a taxpayer puts the reasonableness of expenditures in issue in the Notice of Appeal and the Crown omits any challenge to reasonableness in its Reply, the Court will not consider a later argument that the claim should be reduced for excessive quantum.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

While Feedlot Health Management Services Ltd. v. The Queen represents a landmark victory for Canadian SR&ED claimants regarding the expansive scope of "in respect of" under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II), relying on judicial intervention under R. v. Mian or Crown pleading omissions is an untenable tax planning strategy. Claimants should also note that the statutory wording on which the Court relied has since changed: section 8(1) of the Budget Implementation Act, 2017, No. 2, S.C. 2017, c. 33 (assented to December 14, 2017), replaced the English version of clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) so that, for expenditures incurred after September 16, 2016, it refers to an expenditure "for" rather than "in respect of" the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer, and section 5 of the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3, further amended the clause so that it also applies to expenditures of a capital nature, in respect of property acquired on or after December 16, 2024. Because Justice Woods expressly distinguished expenditures "for" SR&ED from the broader category of expenditures "in respect of" SR&ED, current claims under clause (II) cannot rest on the breadth of the former wording, and the payments must be shown to be for the prosecution of the third-party SR&ED itself. The following two hypothetical, illustrative industry case studies (the companies and individuals described are fictional and do not appear in the decision) demonstrate step-by-step how Canadian corporate taxpayers confronting the exact operational, commercial, and contractual pitfalls identified in 2015 TCC 32 can proactively structure their project governance, technical documentation, contract architecture, and cost-tracking protocols to withstand CRA technical and financial audit scrutiny.
4.1 Case Study One: Commercial Aquaculture Biopharmaceutical and Feed Formulation Trials
4.1.1 Fact Pattern and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Pacific Salmonid Genomics Inc. ("PSGI"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation based in British Columbia, conducts veterinary biotechnology research developing novel immunomodulatory feed additives and sea-lice peptide vaccines for Atlantic salmon. PSGI elects the proxy method on Form T661 to claim its SR&ED expenditures and ITCs under section 127. To validate efficacy across commercial marine densities, PSGI requires access to 50,000 juvenile salmon smolts raised to market weight in ocean net-pens over an extended multi-month cycle.

PSGI's founder and 42.5% indirect shareholder, Dr. Helena Vance, also owns 100% of Coastal Pelagic Farms Ltd. ("Coastal Farms"), a commercial salmon producer that owns the biological fish stock and sells harvested salmon to commercial seafood packing houses. Coastal Farms houses its fish at marine net-pen sites operated by an independent aquaculture management contractor, Fjord Marine Services Ltd. ("Fjord Marine"). Initially, PSGI's external accountant drafted a single contract between PSGI and Coastal Farms titled "Biomass Lease & Feed Consumption Agreement," under which PSGI agreed to pay Coastal Farms $1,200,000 characterized in the contract text as "reimbursement for all experimental fish feed and health costs consumed and lease of 50,000 salmon". In actual practice, however, the $1,200,000 payment was calculated as a negotiated fixed fee of $24 per fish designed to compensate Coastal Farms for the biological and economic risks of subjecting its commercial stock to experimental dietary and harvest timing constraints.

Under the principles established in 2015 TCC 32, PSGI faces severe audit exposure across three fronts. First, claiming the $1,200,000 as "materials consumed" under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) is unlikely to succeed: although the Court in FHMS did not rule on that characterization, under the CRA's administrative policy the feed would not be regarded as consumed because it is metabolized into commercial salmon sold by Coastal Farms, and the written agreement misstates the actual per-fish risk fee negotiated by the parties, inviting judicial skepticism toward any self-interested testimony attempting to explain the discrepancy as inadvertent. Claiming the payment as an "equipment lease" under clauses (I) or (VI) will similarly fail because PSGI never takes exclusive possession or physical care of the fish under the common law standard in Johnson v. British Canadian Insurance Company. Second, because Coastal Farms raises and harvests the salmon for commercial sale in the ordinary course of its aquaculture investment business, Coastal Farms' direct activities fall squarely within the commercial production exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(i). Third, unlike the Crown's pleading omission in FHMS, a properly instructed Crown counsel will explicitly plead quantum unreasonableness in the Reply, challenging whether the $24-per-fish fee paid to a 42.5% shareholder's company is excessive relative to the obligations assumed.
4.1.2 Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Restructuring Contractual Architecture to Establish the Clause (II) Tripartite Nexus

To overcome these disqualifications, PSGI must immediately rescind the "Biomass Lease & Feed Consumption Agreement" prior to project commencement and execute two transparent, legally distinct agreements that mirror the tripartite structure that succeeded under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) in FHMS, adapted to the current wording of that clause. First, PSGI must execute a direct Cooperator and Testing Agreement with the independent net-pen operator, Fjord Marine, to perform supporting SR&ED work under paragraph 248(1)(d). This agreement must explicitly obligate Fjord Marine's technicians to administer the experimental peptide vaccines and immunomodulatory feed rations across segregated test and control net-pens according to PSGI's protocols, take periodic biometric measurements and sea-lice counts, and transmit the collected experimental datasets directly to PSGI for statistical analysis.

Second, PSGI must execute a separate Research Study Agreement with Coastal Farms whose recitals and operative clauses explicitly anchor the contract to the third-party SR&ED performed by Fjord Marine. Under this agreement, Coastal Farms covenants to acquire at its own expense 50,000 smolts with specific genetic and health characteristics suitable for the study and deliver them to Fjord Marine's participating net-pens, while paying all acquisition, transport, and pre-acceptance feeding costs until PSGI confirms the fish meet study specifications. Once accepted into the study, Coastal Farms grants PSGI full access to all health and post-harvest carcass data and cedes complete authority over all health, feeding, and marketing decisions—including dictating when the fish are sent to the packing plant to fit project requirements. Crucially, all fictional references to "feed consumed" or "equipment leases" must be eliminated from the contract text. Instead, the payment clause must accurately state the true negotiated fixed fee per fish and specify that the payment is incurred solely to secure and deliver test subjects to Fjord Marine's facility for the prosecution of the third-party SR&ED testing and data collection directly undertaken by Fjord Marine on behalf of PSGI pursuant to clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II).
Step 2: Segregating Commercial Production Costs from Incremental SR&ED Risk Costs

To insulate the payments to Coastal Farms against a quantum reasonableness challenge and to keep the payments clearly tied to the third-party SR&ED rather than to Coastal Farms' commercial production (bearing in mind that, under FHMS, paragraph 248(1)(i) evaluates the work performed rather than the payments made), PSGI must implement a rigorous valuation methodology appended directly to the Research Study Agreement. Under this framework, Coastal Farms remains financially responsible for standard commercial smolt acquisition and baseline commercial husbandry costs. PSGI's fixed per-fish fee to Coastal Farms is mathematically derived from and restricted to verifiable experimental risks and incremental disruptions: the exact wholesale value of fish sacrificed for destructive histological necropsy prior to commercial harvest; documented mortality or weight-gain suppression in experimental and negative-control pens exceeding Coastal Farms' historical commercial baseline; and verified market-price penalties suffered by Coastal Farms because PSGI mandated harvesting the cohort outside peak seasonal pricing windows to satisfy experimental endpoints.
Step 3: Project Governance and Contemporaneous Technical Documentation

To establish the evidentiary foundation required by the Tax Court of Canada, PSGI's project governance must enforce strict separation between routine aquaculture husbandry and systematic experimental investigation. PSGI must draft a formal pre-trial scientific protocol documenting why the immunological and nutritional interactions of the new vaccine and feed additive cannot be predicted in advance, establishing the systematic, unproven experimental nature of the regime—while recognizing that, under FHMS, describing a protocol as "new" rather than "improved" does not by itself avoid paragraph 248(1)(i), which expressly covers both new and improved products and processes. Fjord Marine's technicians must record contemporaneous activity logs segregating routine commercial feeding from paragraph 248(1)(d) biometric measurement and data collection tasks. Finally, because Dr. Vance holds a 42.5% indirect stake in PSGI and 100% of Coastal Farms, PSGI should obtain a contemporaneous independent valuation report prior to executing the RSAs certifying that the per-fish risk compensation fee reflects reasonable arm's length consideration relative to the commercial risks assumed by Coastal Farms, thereby neutralizing any properly pleaded Crown challenge to quantum reasonableness.
4.2 Case Study Two: In-Situ Industrial Bioprocessing and Commercial Feed Mill Scale-Up Trials
4.2.1 Fact Pattern and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Prairie Agri-Biotech Corp. ("PABC"), an agricultural chemical and bioprocessing engineering firm based in Calgary, Alberta, is developing a novel enzymatic detoxification treatment and steam-pelleting process designed to eliminate mycotoxins and optimize nutrient bioavailability in distressed barley and distillers' grain rations for livestock. Laboratory bench-scale tests cannot replicate the thermal shear, moisture gradients, and biological throughput of an industrial feed processing facility and commercial livestock trial.

To resolve these technological uncertainties, PABC arranges a four-month trial utilizing 4,500 tonnes of specialty grain and cattle owned by Heartland Agri-Investments Ltd. ("Heartland"), a commercial agricultural producer. The grain processing and livestock feeding trials are physically executed inside an industrial mill and feedlot facility operated by an independent third-party contractor, Foothills Custom Processing & Testing Ltd. ("Foothills Testing"). Following the trial, the processed rations and finished livestock are sold by Heartland into normal commercial supply chains. PABC elects the proxy method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and initially signs a "Facility & Commodity Lease Agreement" with Heartland, agreeing to pay Heartland $950,000 described in the agreement as "lease of commercial processing equipment and reimbursement for 4,500 tonnes of grain consumed in testing," even though the parties actually calculated the $950,000 as a fixed risk-indemnity fee per tonne and per animal.

Under Feedlot Health Management Services Ltd. v. The Queen, PABC's initial structure is acutely vulnerable to complete disallowance. First, claiming the $950,000 under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) or (VI) as a lease of equipment will be rejected by the Tax Court because PABC never acquires exclusive possession of either Heartland's biological assets or the industrial facility under Johnson v. British Canadian Insurance Company. Second, claiming the payment as "materials consumed" under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) is untenable because—although FHMS did not rule on that characterization—under the CRA's administrative policy Heartland's commercial commodities, which are sold in its regular commercial business rather than destroyed, would not be regarded as consumed, and the discrepancy between the written "materials consumed" wording and the actual fixed risk fee undermines PABC's evidentiary credibility. Third, because Heartland exploits the output in its regular commercial business, Heartland's direct activities are excluded from SR&ED by paragraph 248(1)(i).
4.2.2 Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Unbundling Truly Consumed Experimental Inputs from Third-Party Access Fees

PABC must first segregate any chemicals or materials that genuinely qualify under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) from the payments made to Heartland. PABC should directly purchase the proprietary experimental enzyme formulations and chemical reagents from chemical suppliers and provide them to Foothills Testing for injection during the experimental runs. Because those experimental enzymes are physically consumed and rendered non-recoverable during the detoxification reactions, their direct acquisition cost legitimately qualifies as "materials consumed" under Clause (V), without tainting the separate contractual arrangements with Heartland.
Step 2: Establishing the Tripartite Contractual Structure Under Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II)

To qualify the $950,000 payment to Heartland under the proxy method, PABC must replace the flawed "Facility & Commodity Lease Agreement" with a tripartite contractual nexus that satisfies clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II). First, PABC must execute a direct Cooperator and Technical Testing Agreement with the facility operator, Foothills Testing, contracting Foothills Testing to perform paragraph 248(1)(d) supporting SR&ED work directly on behalf of PABC. Under this contract, Foothills Testing is obligated to systematically vary thermal conditioning temperatures, enzyme residence times, and ration administration schedules across designated test batches, collect continuous chemical assay and biometric performance data, and transmit the compiled telemetry to PABC's research engineers.

Second, PABC must execute a Test Subject and Feedstock Supply Agreement with Heartland explicitly structured to facilitate Foothills Testing's third-party SR&ED activities. Under this agreement, Heartland agrees to supply the 4,500 tonnes of specific mycotoxin-affected grain and test animals to Foothills Testing's facility at Heartland's own acquisition and transport expense, grant PABC full access to all chemical assay, health, and final yield data, and vest PABC with complete authority over processing parameters, feeding schedules, and marketing timing. The contract text must accurately reflect the negotiated fixed fee per unit and state that the expenditure is paid solely to provide experimental test subjects and feedstock to Foothills Testing for the prosecution of the third-party SR&ED data collection and testing undertaken by Foothills Testing on behalf of PABC.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Yield-Penalty Tracking and Quantum Substantiation

To support the Clause (II) nexus and defeat a properly pleaded Crown challenge to quantum reasonableness, PABC must implement rigorous contemporaneous cost and yield tracking throughout the four-month trial. PABC must document in its technical project records the technological uncertainty and systematic, unproven nature of the enzymatic detoxification parameters—recognizing that, under FHMS, labelling a process "new" rather than "improved" does not by itself avoid paragraph 248(1)(i), which covers both. Furthermore, PABC must substantiate the reasonableness of the $950,000 fee paid to Heartland by linking every invoice to verified experimental disruptions: batches of grain and feed spoiled or rejected due to intentionally boundary-pushing thermal and enzymatic test runs, reduced weight-gain conversion compared to Heartland's commercial control cohorts, and price discounts incurred from delayed marketing schedules mandated by PABC's researchers. By demonstrating that the payments to Heartland strictly compensated for the risks and yield penalties of supplying test subjects to Foothills Testing, PABC establishes a well-documented evidentiary record under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II).
